City of Lafayette 
Staff Report 
City Council 
Date:   June 8, 2026 
Staff:   Niroop K. Srivatsa, City Manager 
Tracy Robinson, Assistant City Manager 
Subject:   FY26-27 Proposed Budget and Workplan Preview 
I N T R O D U C T I O N 
The current City Council goals for FY26-27 are as follows: 
1.   Wildfire prevention, preparedness/responsiveness and utility safety 
2.   Mt. Diablo corridor planning 
3.   Planning for the development and financing of the Citys recreational needs 
Lafayette enters the FY26-27 budget cycle from a position of fiscal strength, due in large part to the 
strong performance of Measure H revenues and continued stability in the Citys core revenue sources. 
Measure H has significantly exceeded original projections and is now generating revenues approaching 
the level of the Citys traditional Bradley-Burns sa les tax. Combined with disciplined spending and 
healthy property and sales tax growth, the Citys   5-year financial forecast now projects balanced 
budgets and reserves above the 60% minimum for the next five years. 
At the same time, the City faces several long-term financial challenges that require continued caution 
and strategic planning. While the City has made important progress in addressing deferred maintenance 
needs and increasing annual sinking fund contributions for buildings, parks, trails, and infrastructure, 
many public assets are aging and will require substantial future investment. Most notably, the 
Community Center has reached a critical stage in its lifecycle, with projected maintenance costs 
exceeding $16 million over the next two decades. In addition, the community continues to express 
strong interest in expanded recreational opportunities, including additional playing fields and enhanced 
recreational facilities. These needs, combined with future obligations such as wildfire prevention 
investments, major transportation and mobility improvements, long-range planning efforts, and 
infrastructure repair projects, underscore the importance of balancing current service levels with long- 
term fiscal sustainability. 
--1--
8:
Against this backdrop, the proposed FY26-27 budget focuses primarily on maintaining existing City 
services and advancing the Councils adopted priorities, while continuing to strengthen the Citys 
financial position   and prepare for significant future capital and infrastructure needs. 
This budget does not include any additional programs or projects and only maintains services at their 
current levels with some minor changes. However, there are three budget requests discussed later in 
this memo.

10:
In addition, the Facilities Assessment concluded that the Community Center will require more than 
$16 million in repairs over the next 20 years, requiring sinking fund contributions of $625K annually 
and escalating by 3.5% each year. This stands in sharp contrast to the historical contribution level of 
approximately $125K per year. 
In January, the Council discussed strategies for funding capital maintenance for City facilities and 
deferred action on the Community Center pending a broader evaluation of long-term options. 
However, the Finance Subcommittee recommended that the City begin increasing contributions 
now, recognizing that significant capital funding will be needed regardless of whether the 
Community Center is ultimately renovated, rebuilt, or relocated. Accordingly, the budget includes 
an additional annual contribution of $500K to Fund 16 for the Community Center sinking fund. 
Changes to community partner contributions -- Chamber, DEIB and LHS: 
The events organized by the Chamber and other community partners play a vital role in 
supporting Lafayettes downtown economy by attr acting visitors who shop locally, dine at 
restaurants, and support local businesses. Recognizing the economic and community value of 
these events, the Council subcommittee recommends that the city, as a partner in economic 
development, contribute personnel time and related costs, including police and Public Works 
support, that were previously charged to the Chamber. The proposed $30,000 contribution to 
the Chamber would be specifically tied to the planning and delivery of major community events 
such as the Art & Wine Festival, the Res Run, and Taste of Lafayette. 
Funding for the Historical Society at $8K and DEIB at $2.5K along with agreements with each to 
provide specific community services and events in exchange. 
Increased the annual amounts transferred from Measure H and the General Fund for Road & Drain 
projects (Fund 14) by 3.5% to mirror the annual inflation increases recommended for the deferred 
maintenance contributions. 
Added funds to City Council (11-110) for election s ($70K) and SB827  Mandated Ethics & Fiscal 
Training ($8.4K), and Phase 2 of the infrastructure assessment project ($50K). 
Moved M3 study ($300K) to Engineering Services (11-420) from Planning (11-410). While this study 
encompasses both transportation and urban planning elements, the Transportation Manager will be 
coordinating the effort. Accordingly, 25% of th e Transportation Managers time has been moved 
from Trans/Circ (11-120) to Engineering Services so that the proposed allocation of funds is 
appropriate and consistent   with the projects mana gement responsibilities. 
Multisport resurfacing ($60K) and installation of bottle fillers/drinking fountains ($12.5K) at the

Community Center. 
$135K for additional infrastructure support for the BART Art Project previously approved by Council 
($135K) and added 4 hours/week for the Administrative Assistant to manage this project in addition 
to the mural projects in process ($7K). 
Consolidated total police costs by combining Traffic Enforcement (11-215) and Supplementary Law 
Enforcement (Fund 73) into Police Services (11-210). Federal SLESF revenue will still be recorded 
into Fund 73 then transferred to the General Fund. 
Following the School District's decision to discontinue its funding and management of the Crossing 
Guard program, the City assumed full program responsibility. The budget is now $164K -- $44K 
more than the previous year. This cost reflects cutting services from 11 locations to 7 locations. 
Added $50K for a compensation study to realign salary benchmarking with current job descriptions 
and organizational needs. The City has not completed a comprehensive review since 2013. With 
labor negotiations approaching in advance of the June 2027 MOU expiration, an independent 
assessment will provide an objective basis for any compensation decisions as well as ensure the 
Citys compensation structure remains   competitive and internally consistent. 
B U D G E T   R E Q U E S T S 
There are several budget requests: 
1 .   One of the Councils primary goals is   planning for the development and financing of the Citys 
recreational needs including options for replacing/rebuilding the Community Center. To aid in this 
effort, PTR has requested $350K for a   Master Plan Needs Assessment. 
2 .   Under Federal ADA law, municipalities are required to provide an ADA Transition Plan if the entity 
has 50 or more employees. While the City has had more than that if temporary and part-time 
employees are included, we dont have a formal plan although the Engineering staff does include 
new ADA-compliant infrastructure as part of their CIP projects when appropriate.   Staff estimates 
that contracting a formal plan will cost approximately $100K. 
3 .   Given that Measure H revenues have exceeded projections, staff recommends Council consider 
expanding fire safety programs and projects to further advance one of the central commitments 
made to voters during the Measure H campaign. Public safety staff has prepared a list of potential 
projects and rough costs. Staff recommends letting the Emergency Preparedness Commission 
prioritize the projects with a set budget of up to $250K from Measure H fund balances. 
--5--
12:
5 - Y E A R F O R E C A S T 
The 5-Year forecast has improved from showing deficits of over $200K per year to basically balanced 
budgets for the next five years that are above the 60% reserve threshold. However, the reserve steadily 
decreases from 76% in FY27 to a projected 66% in FY31. 
B O T T O M L I N E 
The City's improved fiscal position  driven primar ily by Measure H -- is encouraging, but the $3.7 million 
in reserves above the 60% threshold should not be viewed as available discretionary funding. Several 
significant capital and infrastructure needs are on the horizon without dedicated funding sources  and 
when costs are fully scoped, they are likely to consume much or all of that cushion. 
Most notably, the aging Community Center has reached a critical inflection point. With projected 
maintenance costs exceeding $16 million over the next 20 years, the City must evaluate whether 
continued repair is the right long-term investment, or whether the community's recreational needs are 
better served by a rebuilt or reconfigured facility. Beyond the Community Center, Engineering staff has 
identified several large infrastructure repair projects that will need to be addressed in the coming years, 
including bridge repairs and additional funding for   the West Reach project. Longer-term obligations  
including the Multimodal Mobility(M3) Study recommendations, the Aqueduct Pathway, a General Plan 
update, and the Housing Element 7th Cycle update  will add further pressure on future budgets. 
Driven by Measure H revenues and disciplined spending, the 5-year model projects balanced budgets 
and reserves above the 60% threshold through FY31. But th at margin is not a surplus to be spent  it is 
a buffer against the substantial investments that lie ahead. Staff recommends that any use of reserves 
above the 60% threshold be evaluated against these known future needs, rather than allocated to 
programs or projects outside the Council's adopted priorities. The most responsible use of the City's 
current fiscal strength is to preserve flexibility for what is coming.
